item.title: Get the Life-Saving Guidance You Need from Your Higher Self — Sun Aug 9, 11:00 AM
item.description:
Raleigh & Triangle Activities Meetup Group What if you had the most wonderful powerful friend always ready to help you live happily every after? Good news, you do, and it’s your own higher self! “Yeah right,” says the closed heart. Well, it’s okay to feel your doubts, fears, and hurts. They don’t make your higher self not exist, but they can block you from experiencing their love. That’s how you become your own creator; you filter the true perfect creation through your own belief choices, including the false negative beliefs that make you miserable. Whenever you’ve had enough, you can turn around to start healing from where you are now. You’re always good enough to learn powerful lessons in how life really works, by understanding and forgiving the mistakes that you already made. It’s never too late to live happily, thanks to a positive Universe full of real higher friends who love, protect, and guide you as much you let them.

The Daily Planet Café is open 5–8pm with a full menu during the Science Café. Join us in-person or watch the livestream on YouTube. The Cape Fear River is North Carolina’s largest river system and the most industrialized in the state. Living in the Lower Cape Fear River is North Carolina’s tiniest fish, the least killifish. item.description:
The Nasher Teen Council is currently accepting applications for the 2026 – 2027 school year! The Nasher Teen Council (NTC) is a free after-school program for Durham County high school students. The NTC meets every Thursday evening throughout the school year (October – April) from 5:30 – 7:30 PM, with the exception of breaks and holidays. Snacks, dinner, and parking are provided at all meetings. During the 2026 – 2027 school year, the NTC will curate an exhibition focused on the environment, climate, and sustainability! Applications are due September 13, 2026 by 11:59 PM.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Fri Nov 6 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. item.description: Take a glance through recent news or social media and you would be hard-pressed not to see mentions of chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) methods aimed at generating text, images and other content. Recent work by Eloundou and colleagues (2023) explored the potential impact of these types of generative AI on labor markets, and survey research, specifically was among the top two most impacted industries. Professor Andrew Ng has been cited as saying “AI won’t replace human workers, but ‘people that use it will replace people that don’t.’” Much of the way researchers in the social sciences and survey research are incorporating AI into their workflow involves some type of prompting. Prompt Engineering approaches along with more nuanced fine tuning approaches are being used and refined to better incorporate more robust approaches for AI incorporation into the research process.
